extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians writing research articles (graduate students and early-career researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for composing clear, readable mathematical research papers: planning, introductions, narrative structure, notation, proofs, figures, grammar, citation practices, and community norms. Aimed at helping authors guide readers through technical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The choices you make when writing your article should depend on who you hope will read it. To ground yourself, imagine you are writing for a specific person who might read your article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What is your reader’s background? What motivation will they need to put your results in context? How much detail would they appreciate seeing in an argument? (Authors note examples: graduate students may write for a particular fellow student.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a detailed outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing a longer article, try to begin with a plan for the sections, main lemmas, and theorems. You can fill in the proofs later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that adding detail may force reorganization; be ready to ruthlessly revise. To help make an outline, explain your work to a friend — this forces you to see the big picture and highlights. Expect to reorganize when proofs are filled in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose notation well
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad notation is the easiest way to lose your reader, and also the easiest mistake to avoid!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard notation in the field and give related names to related objects. Ensure external and internal consistency. When coauthoring or if notation is undecided, be prepared to change it later; prefer defining LaTeX macros rather than global find-and-replace to avoid errors and missed instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: Get to the point
rubrics_metrics.description: Showcase your exciting new results as soon as possible in the introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's OK to postpone definitions to a later 'Notation' section if standard enough. The introduction should cater to casual browsers and specialists: most readers only read the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: Make your results stand out
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easy to miss a main result hidden in the middle of a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theorem environments or separate paragraphs so busy readers can scan for main results quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: Place your results in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how your work fits in with and diverges from previous approaches by highlighting novel contributions and illustrating the broader landscape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MathSciNet/Google Scholar to find related work; be generous in citing related articles to help readers situate your results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: Paint a clear roadmap
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline the remaining sections in the paper and highlight the main arguments in each section and how they fit together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing this structure helps readers sketch an outline of the entire paper and prepares them for lengthy technical articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding text: Introduce each section
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin every section with a sentence indicating what will be done in that section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reorients readers and contextualizes where the current section fits into the larger argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding text: Highlight hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear in your proofs where each of the hypotheses is being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivate hypotheses by providing counterexamples showing what fails when assumptions are removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding text: Include a running example
rubrics_metrics.description: Using one or two well-chosen running examples can help readers digest new concepts and anchor them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate main ideas of long technical arguments and save the reader reorientation time. If unsure which example to include, use the minimal interesting example you worked out while discovering the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing cognitive load: Break up long arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Subdivide long proofs using lemmas so the reader doesn't have to hold too much at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's OK to use a lemma only once. The goal is to minimize what the reader must keep in mind at one time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing cognitive load: Say what to remember and what to forget
rubrics_metrics.description: If a section contains several results but only one is needed later, mention which one is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frees memory in the reader's head and helps them focus on later-important facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing cognitive load: Keep theorem statements short (within reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cluttered theorems can make it difficult to see what is being proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reduce clutter: (a) define terms before the theorem; (b) isolate complicated technical hypotheses in a separate labeled environment. However, if a hypothesis is not a standing assumption, include it near the theorem — do not sacrifice clarity for brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing cognitive load: Keep sentences simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences with a single idea are easier to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine sentences only if it clarifies logic. Prioritize readability and mathematical clarity over stylistic flow; short sentences that appear choppy are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing cognitive load: Start with a warm-up
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof naturally breaks into parts, do the easier parts first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially helpful when easy and hard parts use similar ideas — starting with easier parts builds reader intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing cognitive load: Anticipate what your readers will forget
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use a definition after a long gap, give a reference or include a notation section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal to readers when a term is being reused after some time so they don't have to flip back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clutter in symbols and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use extra symbols only if they help your reader parse expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize parentheses (e.g., log x better than log(x); omit parentheses when traditional such as sin 2x). Avoid gratuitous multiplication symbols (centered dot) unless necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures when helpful and accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider supplementing written arguments with schematics or diagrams to clarify complicated setups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with colors — make diagrams accessible to color-blind readers and usable in black-and-white print (avoid red/green). Write the complete argument first and then supplement with figures; do not replace essential parts of an argument with a picture alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring proofs: Declare your variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce new notation before using it in a formula so the reader does not need to cycle back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing, search for ', where' and rephrase. Prefer sentences like 'Let x be a real number. Then x^2 + 1 ≥ 0.' instead of 'We have x^2 + 1 ≥ 0, where x is any real number.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring proofs: Avoid unnecessary proofs by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction add temporary hypotheses that make it harder to track active assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, rephrase as a direct proof or a contrapositive. If unavoidable, isolate the subargument in its own paragraph or lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring proofs: Explain the 'obvious'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'clear', 'obvious', 'trivial' as sole justification for a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sentence or two rarely takes long to explain why something is clear; explaining 'trivial' steps helps correctness and avoids hidden errors (anecdote: false claims preceded by 'clearly').

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: Don’t leave your reader hanging
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sentence contains a claim that will be justified later, signal that the explanation will follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End such sentences with phrases like ', as we now explain.' So the reader knows whether an explanation will follow or when a justification is deferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: Clearly connect reasons and conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single assertion takes more than a few sentences to explain, consider turning it into a lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If turning into a lemma isn't possible, clarify which sentences contain the explanation, and use explicit transitions and references to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: Clarify quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit quantifiers can cause ambiguity (e.g., 'for x ∈ R' might mean 'for some' or 'for all').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve quantifier ambiguity explicitly even when context might make your intent clear to you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: Limit usage of pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pronouns like 'it' sparingly and make sure referents are unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of pronouns can cause readers to lose track of which object is meant; prefer explicit nouns when ambiguity is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: Beware of not-quite synonyms and prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with prepositions: small words like 'so,' 'for,' 'as' can have substantial mathematical implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'so that' to indicate purpose (not to impose a condition — use 'such that'). Avoid using 'as' to mean 'since'; don't use 'per' when you mean 'by'. The paper gives concrete examples of misuse to watch for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: Avoid misplaced modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Place modifiers (like 'only') as close as possible to the word they modify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous placement can change meaning (e.g., 'This set only contains the zero vector' is ambiguous whether 'only' modifies 'this set' or 'contains').

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: State precisely what you prove
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of saying two objects are isomorphic, specify a map between them and claim it is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form is stronger, more usable, and likely what you mean; it avoids vagueness about the isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: Use a single numbering system
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid citation issues and make statements easier to find, use a single numbering system for all theorems, lemmas, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example for amsart: \newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[section] and \newtheorem{lemma}[theorem]{Lemma} in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating ambiguity: Cite precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing other work, include a precise reference to a theorem number or page number (unless you mean to cite the entire work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For arXiv preprints include version number or precise date. For web preprints give URL and date downloaded. Cite version numbers of software or code. Precise citations save readers time when checking references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit feedback to find overlooked ambiguities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguities that seem fine in talks may appear on paper because verbal cues are lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another person can easily find ambiguities; solicit feedback from a friend or mentor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math and grammar: Structure sentences so verbs are words, not symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: The main verb of your sentence should be written out in words, not in symbols; avoid splitting the subject across a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example problematic sentence: 'For an elliptic curve y^2 = x^3+ax+b, the discriminant ∆ = −16(4a^3 + 27b^2).' Replace symbols used as verbs with words such as 'equals'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math and grammar: Use consistent punctuation with displayed equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same punctuation in a sentence with a displayed equation as with an inline equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A displayed equation at the end of a sentence should end with a period; the line before a displayed equation often does not need to end in a colon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math and grammar: Avoid shorthand abbreviations in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use abbreviations like WLOG, iff, and s.t. in your writing; write out English words for logical symbols unless used in formal logic equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'without loss of generality', 'if and only if', 'such that', and write logical quantifiers in words outside formal logic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math and grammar: Do not start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting sentences with symbols may cause readers to miss the sentence boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite to begin with words; avoid lines that begin with a mathematical symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math and grammar: Capitalize theorem/definition/section only by number
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the word 'theorem' (or 'definition' or 'section') only when referring to a theorem by number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lowercase otherwise to follow conventional usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math and grammar: Use numerals for numbers in math papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use numerals for numbers in math papers; small counting numbers can be spelled out if not representing a mathematical quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'consider two genus 2 curves....' use numerals for mathematical quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math and grammar: Prefix 'non' without hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefix 'non' before a common math word does not usually need a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'nonempty', 'nontrivial', 'nonzero' without hyphens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community practice: Cite 'forthcoming' only when preprint is publicly available
rubrics_metrics.description: Announced results which take a very long time to appear (or never appear) are detrimental; cite 'forthcoming work' only if a publicly available preprint exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is consistent with AMS Ethical Guidelines [1, Section I].

rubrics_metrics.name: Community practice: Avoid 'microslights' and be mindful of inclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to make proofs followable ('microslights') can deter those prone to doubt themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissive wording like 'trivial' without guidance; use phrases such as 'a standard calculation involving ... shows...' to convey novelty while pointing readers in the right direction. Be mindful that your writing affects the inclusivity of the mathematical community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closing practice: Use revision strategies and external readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing and revising can be lengthy; enlist a second pair of eyes or step away for fresh perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider rewriting drafts from scratch as part of convergence (anecdote: Serre); invest effort to balance clarity and length (the 'golden ratio').
